title: From Issue Numbers to Archival Call Numbers: comparative addressing systems for microscope-slide collections
research_problem: Microscope slides survive historically because successive people and institutions make them retrievable. The same physical preparation can move through commercial, serial, laboratory, cabinet, museum, and archival address systems. Those address changes alter what relations remain visible.
working_claim: A microscope slide becomes historically legible through addresses. Numbers, labels, trays, ledgers, cards, catalogues and call numbers are not ancillary metadata: they are infrastructures that bind a fragile object to texts, people, places, methods and other objects. When an address system changes, some relations are preserved, some are translated, and some disappear.
guard: Address is used analytically for an explicit retrieval or cross-reference coordinate. It does not imply that every historical number served the same function, and it must not collapse catalogue numbers, accession numbers, serial numbers, cabinet coordinates, archive signaturae, and modern database IDs into one namespace.

comparative_dimensions.dimension: Is the address fixed or mutable?

research_consequences: Do not normalize historical identifiers into one master number. Store every namespace and the evidence for transitions between them.
A missing crosswalk is itself a historical result: the object may survive while the relation that made it usable in an earlier system has disappeared.
Collection catalogues should be read as active technologies of retrieval and maintenance, not passive descriptions of holdings.
Labels deserve transcription as documents. Pacini and Cajal show that labels can contain method, time, interpretation, storage history and publication relations.

Cabinet order and archival order answer different questions. A cabinet can optimize use or replacement; an archive can optimize custody; a publication can optimize serial reading. Moving between them can change the epistemic identity of the same piece of glass.
The global comparison does not need identical institutions. Its controlled variable is the act of making physical microscopic preparations retrievable across changing documentary systems.

article_or_book_payoff.cole_article: Keep Cole as the main historical case. Cajal, Pacini, Tempère–Peragallo and Grunow should appear only as short comparative endpoints unless the article is expanded into a broader history of material publication.
article_or_book_payoff.slides_project: Use 'address history' as a derived analytical layer across the object survey: preserve original number, series number, label number, cabinet/tray, accession, old catalogue, present accession/database ID, and documented transitions.
article_or_book_payoff.future_article: A separate comparative paper could study how scientific collections survive by changing addresses, using Cole/Croydon, Cajal, Pacini, Grunow, Van Heurck and La Plata as structurally different cases.
